chapters.s: The opening chapter frames Garh Narikel through the shell-silver problem: error, the enduring sense of “I”, and competing accounts of illusion are dramatized before the argument extends from mistaken perception to the status of the visible world in relation to the Self.
chapters.g: This chapter follows the central epistemological argument of the opening, adhyāsa, section of Vachaspati Mishra’s Bhamati: an analysis of the experience of “I”; the three classical accounts of illusion—Nyaya anyathākhyāti, Prabhakara akhyāti, and the Advaitin account of anirvacanīya-khyāti, established here through the examples of shell-silver and mirage-water…

chapters.s: Udayana’s arguments are staged against a composite Buddhist opponent: momentariness and mind-only claims are tested, while memory and self-awareness become grounds for defending an enduring Self and opening the question of liberation.
chapters.g: This chapter follows the four principal movements of Udayana’s Atmatattvaviveka: the critique of universal momentariness, the critique of the denial of external objects (Vijñanavada), the positive proof of the Self principally through self-awareness and memory, and the treatise’s turn toward God and liberation.…

chapters.s: The disputation turns from the Self to the world and its cause. Competing explanations of creation and causation are tested as the philosophical prehistory of Garh Narikel continues to connect abstract proof with the later ethics of witness.

Gangesha’s Tattvachintamani becomes a dramatic method of successive objection and refinement: auspicious invocation, valid cognition, shell-silver error, vyapti and inference to God demonstrate how claims must survive increasingly exact tests.
chapters.g: This chapter follows four representative movements of Gangesha Upadhyaya’s Tattvachintamani: the opening debate over the causal efficacy of auspicious invocation, including the treatise’s own reference to Udayana’s absent-minded completion of the Kiranavali; the progressive definition of valid cognition (pramanya) through the classical shell-silver error…

In Purva-Mimamsa, the sole authority for dharma is the Vedic injunctive sentence: an act not explicitly enjoined in the Veda does not fall within the category of dharma.…
Indian philosophy preserves three major accounts of the nature of illusion. The Nyaya-Vaisheshika school accepts anyathākhyāti: in error, both objects—the shell and the silver—are real…
